newsitem.title: UK: POLL - Hefty gilt payments, weak VAT to hit UK PSBR.
newsitem.headline: POLL - Hefty gilt payments, weak VAT to hit UK PSBR.

text.p: Britain's public sector debt is expected to increase by four billion pounds ($6.8 billion) or more in June as hefty interest payments on government bonds and weak VAT returns hit the public finances.

A Reuter poll of economists produced a consensus forecasting a public sector borrowing requirement of 4.1 billion stg in June, just above May's 4.0 billion revenue shortfall. The data are due at 0830 GMT on Wednesday.
The picture could have been worse were it not for 700 million pounds of revenue from the second call on the shares of privatised UK rail infrastructure giant, Railtrack Plc.

"Privatisation proceeds from...Railtrack will have inflated the Treasury's coffers during June, although this must be offset against the usual surge in interest payments," said David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders. He expected a four billion stg PSBR, level with May's.

The Office for National Statistics said last month that June is increasingly a peak month for interest payments because gilts are now being issued with aligned coupon dates in June and December. Interest of 2.7 billion stg will have to be paid this June compared with 1.5 billion in June last year.
The ONS also said value-added-tax receipts last month were expected to be lower than the same month last year. In June 1996, Britain's PSBR totalled 3.8 billion stg.
Darshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets, said the weakness of VAT returns reflects changes in the timing of payments, announced in the November 1996 budget.
In May, VAT receipts fell by 11.4 percent year-on-year. "We have allowed for receipts to be almost three percent lower than last June," she said, pencilling in a 4.8 billion PSBR overall.
But the VAT timing effect will mean a balancing rebound in sales tax receipts in July, said Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers.
He forecast a yawning 5.2 billion stg gap between government expenditure and revenue last month, but said there was little cause for concern.
"Such a figure would not stop the PSBR overshooting the Treasury's 10.9 billion forecast significantly over the full fiscal year," he said. "We expect a seven billion PSBR."
The Red Book from Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's first budget on July 2 forecast a 1997/98 PSBR of 10.9 billion pounds.
Excluding the first tranche of the windfall levy, which will be paid by Britain's privatised utilities in December, the PSBR is expected to total 13.3 billion pounds this financial year.
"The government's new forecast for the full-year PSBR is a realistic one," Philpotts said.
